claim: Apicobasal cell polarity loss is a founding event in epithelial–mesenchymal transition and epithelial tumorigenesis.
source: Apicobasal cell polarity loss is a founding event in epithelial–mesenchymal transition and epithelial tumorigenesis, yet how pathological polarity loss links to plasticity remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding in the field, representing consensus knowledge about the role of polarity loss in EMT and tumorigenesis.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed of Drosophila ovaries where inducing polarity-gene l(2)gl-knockdown causes invasive multilayering of the follicular epithelia.
source: To understand the mechanisms and mediators regulating plasticity upon polarity loss, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of Drosophila ovaries, where inducing polarity-gene l(2)gl-knockdown (Lgl-KD) causes invasive multilayering of the follicular epithelia.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach taken, which is supported by the data generated in the study.

claim: Cells specific to various discernible phenotypes were discovered by analyzing integrated Lgl-KD and wildtype transcriptomes.
source: Analyzing the integrated Lgl-KD and wildtype transcriptomes, we discovered the cells specific to the various discernible phenotypes and characterized the underlying gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational analysis of the scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Keap1-Nrf2 signaling has a genetic requirement in promoting multilayer formation of Lgl-KD cells.
source: A genetic requirement of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling in promoting multilayer formation of Lgl-KD cells was further identified.
evidence: This is supported by genetic manipulation experiments showing that knockdown of Keap1 or Nrf2 affects multilayer formation.

claim: Ectopic expression of Keap1 increased the volume of delaminated follicle cells.
source: Ectopic expression of Keap1 increased the volume of delaminated follicle cells that showed enhanced invasive behavior with significant changes to the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of delaminated epithelial volume in Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE egg chambers.

claim: Ectopic expression of Keap1 in Lgl-KD cells showed enhanced invasive behavior with significant changes to the cytoskeleton.
source: Ectopic expression of Keap1 increased the volume of delaminated follicle cells that showed enhanced invasive behavior with significant changes to the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is supported by F-actin staining and quantification showing increased F-actin intensity in multilayers.

claim: The study describes the comprehensive transcriptome of cells within the follicle cell tumor model at single-cell resolution.
source: Overall, our findings describe the comprehensive transcriptome of cells within the follicle cell tumor model at the single-cell resolution and identify a previously unappreciated link between Keap1-Nrf2 signaling and cell plasticity at early tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is a previously unappreciated link between Keap1-Nrf2 signaling and cell plasticity at early tumorigenesis.
source: Overall, our findings describe the comprehensive transcriptome of cells within the follicle cell tumor model at the single-cell resolution and identify a previously unappreciated link between Keap1-Nrf2 signaling and cell plasticity at early tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the novel findings from genetic manipulation and transcriptomic analysis of Keap1-Nrf2 pathway components.

claim: Apical–basal cell polarity acts as a major gatekeeper against tumorigenesis in epithelial tissues.
source: Apical–basal cell polarity acts as a major gatekeeper against tumorigenesis in epithelial tissues (Royer and Lu, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cell polarity dysregulation is commonly associated with tumors.
source: While its dysregulation is commonly associated with tumors (Chatterjee and Deng, 2019; Rudrapatna et al., 2012), cell polarity disruption is tightly controlled to also allow cellular movement during critical developmental processes such as gastrulation and wound healing (Barriere et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell polarity disruption is tightly controlled to allow cellular movement during critical developmental processes such as gastrulation and wound healing.
source: While its dysregulation is commonly associated with tumors (Chatterjee and Deng, 2019; Rudrapatna et al., 2012), cell polarity disruption is tightly controlled to also allow cellular movement during critical developmental processes such as gastrulation and wound healing (Barriere et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Regulation of cell polarity enables cells to undergo changes in plasticity.
source: This regulation of cell polarity enables the cells to undergo changes in plasticity, which is the ability of cells to change their phenotype in response to environmental factors without acquiring genetic mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about cell polarity and plasticity.

claim: Plasticity is the ability of cells to change their phenotype in response to environmental factors without acquiring genetic mutations.
source: This regulation of cell polarity enables the cells to undergo changes in plasticity, which is the ability of cells to change their phenotype in response to environmental factors without acquiring genetic mutations.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Plasticity in cells facilitates epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition causing them to lose apical–basal polarity and weaken cell–cell adhesion.
source: Plasticity in these cells facilitates epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) causing them to lose apical–basal polarity and weaken cell–cell adhesion with the purpose of promoting their movement beyond the confined space of the tissue (Moreno-Bueno et al., 2008; Plygawko et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EMT is associated with behaviors such as increased invasiveness and metastatic migration of cancer cells.
source: For these reasons, EMT is also associated with behaviors such as increased invasiveness and metastatic migration of cancer cells (Brabletz et al., 2018; Mani et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a continuum of metastable cells undergoing partial-EMT in cancer tissues, instead of one stable state of either epithelial or mesenchymal identity.
source: Recently emerging consensus in the field of EMT research draws attention to the presence of a continuum of metastable cells undergoing partial-EMT in cancer tissues, instead of one stable state of either epithelial or mesenchymal identity (Grigore et al., 2016; Saxena et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature representing emerging consensus.

claim: A significant gap exists in understanding how different metastable cell states are supported by underlying gene expression and how it determines the overall behavior of tumor cells.
source: A significant gap exists in our understanding of how these different metastable cell states are supported by the underlying gene expression and how it determines the overall behavior of the tumor cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, representing a knowledge gap.

claim: Epithelial polarity is maintained by mutually antagonizing, spatially restricted protein complexes at the apical and basolateral cytosolic domains of the cell.
source: Epithelial polarity is maintained by the mutually antagonizing, spatially restricted protein complexes at the apical and basolateral cytosolic domains of the cell that are frequently found disrupted in several cancers (Elsum et al., 2012; Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Parker et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Polarity protein complexes are frequently found disrupted in several cancers.
source: Epithelial polarity is maintained by the mutually antagonizing, spatially restricted protein complexes at the apical and basolateral cytosolic domains of the cell that are frequently found disrupted in several cancers (Elsum et al., 2012; Huang and Muthuswamy, 2010; Parker et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A causative link between polarity loss and tumorigenesis has been established in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: A causative link between polarity loss and tumorigenesis has since been established in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, where the loss of basolateral polarity proteins – such as Scribble (Scrib), Discs large (Dlg), and Lethal giant larvae (l(2)gl or simply, Lgl) – combined with oncogenic Notch or Ras signaling, causes malignant tumorigenesis in several tissues (Chatterjee and Deng, 2019; Enomoto et al., 2018; Papagiannouli and Mechler, 2004; Papagiannouli and Mechler, 2013; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of basolateral polarity proteins combined with oncogenic Notch or Ras signaling causes malignant tumorigenesis in several Drosophila tissues.
source: A causative link between polarity loss and tumorigenesis has since been established in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, where the loss of basolateral polarity proteins – such as Scribble (Scrib), Discs large (Dlg), and Lethal giant larvae (l(2)gl or simply, Lgl) – combined with oncogenic Notch or Ras signaling, causes malignant tumorigenesis in several tissues (Chatterjee and Deng, 2019; Enomoto et al., 2018; Papagiannouli and Mechler, 2004; Papagiannouli and Mechler, 2013; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several advances have been made in identifying genetic factors that regulate tumorigenesis in the wing-disc tumor model.
source: While several advances have since been made in identifying genetic factors that regulate tumorigenesis in the wing-disc tumor model (Atkins et al., 2016; Dillard et al., 2021; Doggett et al., 2015; Logeay et al., 2022), our understanding of the mechanisms driving neoplastic remodeling of the tissue is lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Understanding of the mechanisms driving neoplastic remodeling of the tissue is lacking.
source: While several advances have since been made in identifying genetic factors that regulate tumorigenesis in the wing-disc tumor model (Atkins et al., 2016; Dillard et al., 2021; Doggett et al., 2015; Logeay et al., 2022), our understanding of the mechanisms driving neoplastic remodeling of the tissue is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The limitation in understanding neoplastic remodeling is due to the use of bulk tissue-based approaches that cannot resolve cellular heterogeneity inherent to the growing tumor.
source: This limitation is due to (1) the use of bulk tissue-based approaches that cannot resolve the cellular heterogeneity inherent to the growing tumor, and (2) rampant malignancy in the wing-disc tumor model that obscures characterization of individual cell behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological limitations in the field.

claim: Rampant malignancy in the wing-disc tumor model obscures characterization of individual cell behavior.
source: This limitation is due to (1) the use of bulk tissue-based approaches that cannot resolve the cellular heterogeneity inherent to the growing tumor, and (2) rampant malignancy in the wing-disc tumor model that obscures characterization of individual cell behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of the wing-disc tumor model.

claim: Phenotypic heterogeneity exists within multilayered follicle cells of Drosophila ovaries where Lgl-knockdown is induced.
source: In a recent study, we drew attention to the phenotypic heterogeneity within multilayered follicle cells of Drosophila ovaries where Lgl-knockdown (Lgl-KD) is induced to cause polarity loss (Jevitt et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Multilayered cells with Lgl-KD displayed continued survival and sustained growth without causing long-distance metastasis when transplanted into the host's abdomen, even in the presence of oncogenic Notch signaling.
source: Even in the presence of oncogenic Notch signaling, these multilayered cells displayed continued survival and sustained growth without causing long-distance metastasis when transplanted into the host's abdomen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from a previous study.

claim: The lack of oncogenic complexity in Lgl-KD multilayered cells provides an opportunity to study the behavior of discrete dysplastic cells upon polarity loss.
source: This lack of oncogenic complexity provides an opportunity to study the behavior of discrete dysplastic cells upon polarity loss and determine how the underlying gene expression might regulate it.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the experimental model.

claim: The normally developing Drosophila follicular epithelium has been instrumental in understanding cellular plasticity that facilitates developmental EMT and collective migration of anterior follicle cells and border cells.
source: The normally developing Drosophila follicular epithelium has been instrumental in our understanding of cellular plasticity that facilitates developmental EMT and collective migration of the anterior follicle cells and border cells (Silver et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas describing the gene expression signatures of individual w1118 follicle cells was published in 2019.
source: In 2019, we published a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas describing the gene expression signatures of individual w1118 follicle cells, which also included the abovementioned cell types (Jevitt et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The w1118 follicle cell dataset was used as a template to isolate Lgl-KD cells that exhibit gene expression divergent from normally developing follicle cells.
source: In this study, we utilized the w1118 follicle cell dataset as a template to isolate Lgl-KD cells that exhibit gene expression that is divergent from that of the normally developing (as in w1118) follicle cells.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach taken in the study.

claim: The transcriptomic signatures of abnormal cells were characterized and validated for their association with distinct phenotypes observed within ovaries containing Lgl-KD follicle cells.
source: We characterized the transcriptomic signatures of these abnormal cells and validated their association with the distinct phenotypes that are observed within the ovaries containing Lgl-KD follicle cells.
evidence: This describes the analytical and validation approach taken in the study.

claim: The oxidative stress-responsive Keap1-Nrf2 signaling pathway was found to be enriched in the multilayered cells.
source: The oxidative stress-responsive Keap1-Nrf2 signaling pathway was found to be enriched in the multilayered cells and unexpectedly, manipulating the expression of both Keap1 and Nrf2 was found to regulate the invasiveness of collective Lgl-KD cells with significant F-actin remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic analysis and marker validation.

claim: Manipulating the expression of both Keap1 and Nrf2 was found to regulate the invasiveness of collective Lgl-KD cells with significant F-actin remodeling.
source: The oxidative stress-responsive Keap1-Nrf2 signaling pathway was found to be enriched in the multilayered cells and unexpectedly, manipulating the expression of both Keap1 and Nrf2 was found to regulate the invasiveness of collective Lgl-KD cells with significant F-actin remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by genetic manipulation experiments and F-actin quantification.

claim: The findings describe the earliest transcriptomic changes within dysplastic cells of the follicular epithelia with polarity loss.
source: Overall, our findings in this study describe the earliest transcriptomic changes within dysplastic cells of the follicular epithelia with polarity loss in its cells and identify novel regulatory pathways that determine plasticity in the invading tumor.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq analysis of Lgl-KD cells.

claim: Novel regulatory pathways that determine plasticity in the invading tumor were identified.
source: Overall, our findings in this study describe the earliest transcriptomic changes within dysplastic cells of the follicular epithelia with polarity loss in its cells and identify novel regulatory pathways that determine plasticity in the invading tumor.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling as a regulator of invasiveness.

claim: Follicle cell-specific RNAi-mediated silencing of Lgl for 72 hr resulted in premature failure of oogenesis.
source: Using the pan follicle cell traffic jam (tj)-Gal4 driver with temperature-sensitive (TS) Gal80 (Gal80TS) repressor to control transcriptional induction, follicle cell-specific RNAi-mediated silencing of Lgl (Lgl-KD) was induced in adult female flies for 72 hr, which resulted in the premature failure of oogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Failure of egg development resulted in the accumulation of degenerated egg chambers within the epithelial sheath.
source: This failure of egg development resulted in the accumulation of degenerated egg chambers within the epithelial sheath (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging showing degenerated egg chambers.

claim: Phospho-Histone 3 accumulation was observed in follicle cells at egg chamber termini during mid-oogenesis when normal follicle cells cease to undergo mitosis.
source: Additionally, phospho-Histone 3 (pH3) accumulation was observed in the follicle cells at the egg chamber termini during mid-oogenesis, when normal follicle cells of the experimental control and Lgl-KD follicle cells in the lateral epithelia cease to undergo mitosis (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by pH3 staining shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cross-section of egg chambers revealed significant multilayering of the epithelia.
source: Cross-section of these egg chambers revealed significant multilayering of the epithelia, where cells exhibited decreased expression of the differentiated follicle cell marker Hindsight (Hnt) (Sun and Deng, 2007) and increased expression of the immature cell marker Cut (López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005), suggesting changes to the expected cell fate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging and marker staining.

claim: Multilayered cells exhibited decreased expression of the differentiated follicle cell marker Hindsight.
source: Cross-section of these egg chambers revealed significant multilayering of the epithelia, where cells exhibited decreased expression of the differentiated follicle cell marker Hindsight (Hnt) (Sun and Deng, 2007) and increased expression of the immature cell marker Cut (López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005), suggesting changes to the expected cell fate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Hnt staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Multilayered cells exhibited increased expression of the immature cell marker Cut.
source: Cross-section of these egg chambers revealed significant multilayering of the epithelia, where cells exhibited decreased expression of the differentiated follicle cell marker Hindsight (Hnt) (Sun and Deng, 2007) and increased expression of the immature cell marker Cut (López-Schier and St Johnston, 2001; Sun and Deng, 2005), suggesting changes to the expected cell fate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Cut staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both Shg and Arm staining displayed gradually decreasing enrichment at multilayered cell junctions along the apical–basal axis.
source: Both Shg and Arm staining displayed gradually decreasing enrichment at the multilayered cell junctions along the apical–basal axis, with the basal-most layer expressing Shg at levels comparable to that observed in the monolayered cells of the experimental control egg chambers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging and staining shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The basal-most layer of multilayered cells expressed Shg at levels comparable to that observed in monolayered cells of experimental control egg chambers.
source: Both Shg and Arm staining displayed gradually decreasing enrichment at the multilayered cell junctions along the apical–basal axis, with the basal-most layer expressing Shg at levels comparable to that observed in the monolayered cells of the experimental control egg chambers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Significant decrease in Shg enrichment was observed along with mildly elevated F-actin at the apical-most tip of the invading group of cells.
source: When the intensities of F-actin (Phalloidin) and Shg were measured along the apical–basal axis of the invasive multilayer shown in Figure 1B, significant decrease in Shg enrichment was observed along with mildly elevated F-actin at the apical-most tip of the invading group of cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Apically invasive movement was detected in single-cell derived, positively marked lglRNAi MARCM clones.
source: Apically invasive movement was also detected in the single-cell derived, positively marked (GFP+) lglRNAi MARCM clones, as well as groups of mitotic clones derived from negatively marked (GFP-) homozygous lgl4 mutant follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Apically invasive movement was detected in groups of mitotic clones derived from negatively marked homozygous lgl4 mutant follicle cells.
source: Apically invasive movement was also detected in the single-cell derived, positively marked (GFP+) lglRNAi MARCM clones, as well as groups of mitotic clones derived from negatively marked (GFP-) homozygous lgl4 mutant follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Multilayering at midoogenesis was the most prevalent large-scale phenotype observed across different stages of oogenesis in tjTS>lglRNAi ovarioles after 72 hr of Lgl-knockdown (83.25%; n = 280).
source: Quantifying our observations across five independent experiments, we found that multilayering at midoogenesis was the most prevalent (83.25%; n = 280) large-scale phenotype observed across the different stages of oogenesis in tjTS>lglRNAi ovarioles after 72 hr of Lgl-knockdown (72h-Lgl-KD) induction (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: About 6.05% of egg chambers displayed fused egg chambers at early oogenesis after 72 hr of Lgl-knockdown.
source: Additionally, about 6.05% (n = 280) of egg chambers displayed fused egg chambers at early oogenesis, while degenerated egg chambers were observed in about half of all egg chambers (51.86%; n = 280) at developmental stages beyond stage 9 or 10 during late oogenesis as a consequence of germline cell death (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Degenerated egg chambers were observed in about half of all egg chambers (51.86%; n = 280) at developmental stages beyond stage 9 or 10 during late oogenesis as a consequence of germline cell death.
source: Additionally, about 6.05% (n = 280) of egg chambers displayed fused egg chambers at early oogenesis, while degenerated egg chambers were observed in about half of all egg chambers (51.86%; n = 280) at developmental stages beyond stage 9 or 10 during late oogenesis as a consequence of germline cell death (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Whole-tissue RNA sequencing analysis was performed of ovarian tissues from both experimental control and Lgl-KD flies with RNAi induction for 24 hr and 96 hr.
source: To test this, we performed whole-tissue RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of ovarian tissues from both experimental control and Lgl-KD flies with RNAi induction for 24 hr (shorter) and 96 hr (longer periods of time).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: 24h-Lgl-KD did not induce observable phenotypic changes.
source: While 24h-Lgl-KD did not induce observable phenotypic changes, 96h-Lgl-KD displayed significant epithelial multilayering and germline cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 96h-Lgl-KD displayed significant epithelial multilayering and germline cell death.
source: While 24h-Lgl-KD did not induce observable phenotypic changes, 96h-Lgl-KD displayed significant epithelial multilayering and germline cell death (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Principal component analysis separated the 96h-Lgl-KD sample from others across principal component 1 (77% variance).
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) comparing all four samples separated the 96h-Lgl-KD sample from others across principal component 1 (PC1; 77% variance), indicating that significant transcriptomic differences separate the sample with the differential phenotype from the rest (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Significant transcriptomic differences separate the 96h-Lgl-KD sample with the differential phenotype from the rest.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) comparing all four samples separated the 96h-Lgl-KD sample from others across principal component 1 (PC1; 77% variance), indicating that significant transcriptomic differences separate the sample with the differential phenotype from the rest (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Several genes associated with late-stage oogenesis showed reduced expression in 96h-Lgl-KD compared to no-phenotype samples.
source: When compared with all these 'no-phenotype' samples collectively, several genes associated with late-stage oogenesis (e.g., Vm26Ac, Femcoat, Cp15, yellow-g, etc.) showed reduced expression, while expression of genes involved in actin binding (Molecular Function GO: 0003779; p=2.843 × 10–3), locomotion (Biological Process GO: 0040011; p=3.748 × 10–11), and cell periphery (Cellular Component GO: 0071944; p=2.904 × 10–19) were found elevated in the 96h-Lgl-KD sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Expression of genes involved in actin binding, locomotion, and cell periphery were found elevated in the 96h-Lgl-KD sample.
source: When compared with all these 'no-phenotype' samples collectively, several genes associated with late-stage oogenesis (e.g., Vm26Ac, Femcoat, Cp15, yellow-g, etc.) showed reduced expression, while expression of genes involved in actin binding (Molecular Function GO: 0003779; p=2.843 × 10–3), locomotion (Biological Process GO: 0040011; p=3.748 × 10–11), and cell periphery (Cellular Component GO: 0071944; p=2.904 × 10–19) were found elevated in the 96h-Lgl-KD sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Apoptotic cell clearance genes croquemort and draper were upregulated in the 96h-Lgl-KD samples.
source: Additionally, apoptotic cell clearance genes, such as croquemort (crq) (0.66 log2FC; p=0.00015) and draper (drpr) (0.642 log2FC; p=0.00027), were also upregulated in the 96h-Lgl-KD samples, likely in response to increased germline cell death at later stages of oogenesis (Etchegaray et al., 2012; Franc et al., 1996; Franc et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: Upregulation of apoptotic cell clearance genes is likely in response to increased germline cell death at later stages of oogenesis.
source: Additionally, apoptotic cell clearance genes, such as croquemort (crq) (0.66 log2FC; p=0.00015) and draper (drpr) (0.642 log2FC; p=0.00027), were also upregulated in the 96h-Lgl-KD samples, likely in response to increased germline cell death at later stages of oogenesis (Etchegaray et al., 2012; Franc et al., 1996; Franc et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data and previous literature.

claim: 16,060 ovarian cells of the tjTS>lglRNAi dataset were grouped into 17 clusters based on gene expression similarities.
source: On the basis of gene expression similarities, 16,060 ovarian cells of the tjTS>lglRNAi dataset were grouped into 17 clusters (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Follicle cells were isolated by positively identifying and removing nonepithelial cell types using previously described markers.
source: Follicle cells were isolated for more targeted analyses by positively identifying nonepithelial cell types using previously described markers (Jevitt et al., 2020) (vasa+ and oskar+ early and late germline cells, Zasp66+ muscle sheath cells and Hml+ macrophage cell population known as the hemocytes) and removing them from the dataset.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach taken in the study.

claim: 14,537 Lgl-KD follicle cells were integrated with 17,875 w1118 follicle cells and collectively assembled into 20 clusters.
source: The remaining 14,537 Lgl-KD follicle cells were then integrated with 17,875 w1118 follicle cells (that were processed similarly to remove nonepithelial cells) and were collectively assembled into 20 clusters (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by integration analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Clusters were annotated according to the differential enrichment of stage- and cell-type-specific marker expression.
source: These clusters were annotated according to the differential enrichment of stage- and cell-type-specific marker expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Clusters of cells belonging to egg chambers at stage 9 and beyond had lower proportions of Lgl-KD cells.
source: Consistent with the phenotypic observation that egg chambers degenerate post-midoogenesis around stage 8, clusters of cells belonging to egg chambers at stage 9 and beyond (clusters 9, 10, 11, 14, and 19) had lower proportions of Lgl-KD cells (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cluster composition analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Clusters 7, 8, 13, 16, and 17 were unique to the Lgl-KD dataset.
source: Significantly, we also identified clusters (clusters 7, 8, 13, 16, and 17) that were unique to the Lgl-KD dataset (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The integration-based approach was able to separate clusters unique to the individual datasets, possibly representative of cells exhibiting diverse stage-specific Lgl-KD phenotypes.
source: Our integration-based approach was thus able to separate clusters unique to the individual datasets, possibly representative of cells exhibiting the diverse stage-specific Lgl-KD phenotypes and the loss of cells from expected stages comparable to the w1118 developmental lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the integration analysis results.

claim: RNA velocity vectors placed clusters 7, 13, 16, and 17 along a linear transition that terminated into cluster 8.
source: The underlying lineage transitions among the cells of unique Lgl-KD clusters were then estimated by dynamically modeling their inherent RNA velocity (Bergen et al., 2020). The resultant stream of velocity vectors placed clusters 7, 13, 16, and 17 along a linear transition that terminated into cluster 8, while cluster 8 itself showed mixed lineage as was suggested by the nonuniform direction of velocity vectors (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cluster 8 showed mixed lineage as suggested by the nonuniform direction of velocity vectors.
source: The resultant stream of velocity vectors placed clusters 7, 13, 16, and 17 along a linear transition that terminated into cluster 8, while cluster 8 itself showed mixed lineage as was suggested by the nonuniform direction of velocity vectors (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Clusters 13, 16 and the near-terminal cells of cluster 7 were the stable end points of the assumed lineage.
source: The latent time experienced by the cells in these clusters as well as the likely terminal endpoints were then inferred from the estimated lineage, which subsequently suggested that clusters 13, 16 and the near-terminal cells of cluster 7 were the stable end points of the assumed lineage while cluster 7 displayed highly dynamic transcriptional transition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on latent time analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cluster 7 displayed highly dynamic transcriptional transition.
source: The latent time experienced by the cells in these clusters as well as the likely terminal endpoints were then inferred from the estimated lineage, which subsequently suggested that clusters 13, 16 and the near-terminal cells of cluster 7 were the stable end points of the assumed lineage while cluster 7 displayed highly dynamic transcriptional transition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on latent time analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The unique clusters were a mix of stable terminal cell states as well as transitioning cell states.
source: Overall, given the uncompacted topology of certain cluster manifolds as well as the results from our linage analysis, we concluded that the unique clusters were a mix of stable terminal cell states as well as transitioning cell states (see 'Methods').
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple analytical approaches.

claim: Apoptotic cell clearance markers drpr and crq were specifically detected in the cells of cluster 8.
source: Apoptotic cell clearance markers drpr (Etchegaray et al., 2012) and crq (Franc et al., 1999), which were previously detected via bulk RNA-seq, were now specifically detected in the cells of cluster 8, while polar and border cell-associated markers (Jevitt et al., 2020), such as unpaired (upd1), slow border cells (slbo), and singed (sn), were found enriched in cluster 17 cells.
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: Polar and border cell-associated markers such as unpaired, slow border cells, and singed were found enriched in cluster 17 cells.
source: Apoptotic cell clearance markers drpr (Etchegaray et al., 2012) and crq (Franc et al., 1999), which were previously detected via bulk RNA-seq, were now specifically detected in the cells of cluster 8, while polar and border cell-associated markers (Jevitt et al., 2020), such as unpaired (upd1), slow border cells (slbo), and singed (sn), were found enriched in cluster 17 cells.
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: Expression of sn and drpr was validated within the multilayers and found to be expressed in polar cells and in follicle cells of egg chambers that associate with dying germline cells, respectively.
source: We validated the expression of sn and drpr within the multilayers and found them to be expressed in the polar cells and in the follicle cells of egg chambers that associate with dying germline cells, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by antibody staining shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Border cell-specific expression of sn implied that once egg chambers have individualized, the polar to border cell fate is not disrupted upon Lgl-KD, despite the impairment of border cell migration.
source: Border cell-specific expression of sn further implied that once the egg chambers have individualized, the polar to border cell fate is not disrupted upon Lgl-KD, despite the impairment of border cell migration.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression validation.

claim: Clusters 13 and 16 represent immature (mitotic) and mature (endocycling) follicle cells based on differential Stg expression.
source: While markers of immature, mitotic follicle cells (Jevitt et al., 2020) such as Myc, Df31, and HmgD were detected in cluster 13, it showed significant overlap with cluster 16, with the notable exception of the Drosophila Cdc25 homolog string (stg) expression. This difference in Stg expression led us to believe that clusters 13 and 16 represent immature (mitotic) and mature (endocycling) follicle cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression analysis.

claim: Very few specific markers were identified for cluster 7 as the markers either shared gene expression with main body follicle cells or clusters 8, 13, and 16.
source: Additionally, very few specific markers were identified for cluster 7 as the markers either shared gene expression with (1) the main body follicle cells (expressing Yp2 and Yp3), suggestive of a shared (and possibly, derivative) lineage, and (2) clusters 8, 13, and 16, exhibiting only quantitative differences between them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transcription factor regulon activity was assessed in the unique Lgl-KD clusters using SCENIC.
source: Instead of focusing on individual gene expression, we assessed the transcription factor (TF) regulon activity in the unique Lgl-KD clusters using SCENIC (Aibar et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the analytical approach taken in the study.

claim: Clusters 7 and 13 showed major differences in the enriched regulons.
source: While clusters 7 and 13 showed major differences in the enriched regulons, we found only two regulons (Hr4 and crc_extended) specific to cluster 7 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by regulon activity analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Only two regulons (Hr4 and crc_extended) were specific to cluster 7.
source: While clusters 7 and 13 showed major differences in the enriched regulons, we found only two regulons (Hr4 and crc_extended) specific to cluster 7 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by regulon activity analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hierarchically grouping the clusters based on scaled regulon activity found cluster 7 to be more similar to cluster 8 than cluster 13.
source: Hierarchically grouping the clusters based on scaled regulon activity found cluster 7 to be more similar to cluster 8 than cluster 13, as was also evident from the relatively lower values for the enrichment of several regulons.
evidence: This is an inference based on hierarchical clustering of regulon activity.

claim: The five most specifically enriched regulons of cluster 7 included the TFs crc, Xbp1, Pdp1, BEAF-32, and CrebA.
source: The five most specifically enriched regulons of cluster 7 included the TFs crc (regulon specificity score [RSS] = 0.42), Xbp1 (0.42), Pdp1 (0.41), BEAF-32 (0.41), and CrebA (0.41) and were identified alongside the AP-1 TFs Jra (0.4) and kay (0.39) that have been reported to drive tumorigenic JNK signaling upon polarity loss (Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by regulon specificity analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: AP-1 TFs Jra and kay have been reported to drive tumorigenic JNK signaling upon polarity loss.
source: The five most specifically enriched regulons of cluster 7 included the TFs crc (regulon specificity score [RSS] = 0.42), Xbp1 (0.42), Pdp1 (0.41), BEAF-32 (0.41), and CrebA (0.41) and were identified alongside the AP-1 TFs Jra (0.4) and kay (0.39) that have been reported to drive tumorigenic JNK signaling upon polarity loss (Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A dynamic gene expression profile was observed in cluster 7 cells.
source: Consolidating the results from marker validation, RNA velocity-based lineage inference and the relative specificity as well as activity of detected regulons, a dynamic gene expression profile was observed in cluster 7 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple analytical approaches.

claim: Cluster 7 cells are derived from both mitotic cells and endocycling cells.
source: These cells are derived from both mitotic cells (as velocity vectors can be seen transitioning from cluster 13 to 7) as well as endocycling cells (given the expression of main body follicle cell markers) and represent a transcriptomic state preceding that of the cluster 8 (that represents cells at a later developmental timepoint), as the enriched regulons show similar specificity but elevated activity from cluster 7 to cluster 8.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA velocity analysis and marker expression.

claim: Cluster 7 represents a transcriptomic state preceding that of cluster 8.
source: These cells are derived from both mitotic cells (as velocity vectors can be seen transitioning from cluster 13 to 7) as well as endocycling cells (given the expression of main body follicle cell markers) and represent a transcriptomic state preceding that of the cluster 8 (that represents cells at a later developmental timepoint), as the enriched regulons show similar specificity but elevated activity from cluster 7 to cluster 8.
evidence: This is an inference based on regulon activity analysis.

claim: JNK signaling-associated AP-1 TFs Jra and kay have been previously implicated in polarity loss-induced metastatic tumor formation in the wing discs.
source: Among the regulons exhibiting elevated activity in cluster 7 than cluster 8, the JNK signaling-associated AP-1 TFs Jra and kay have been previously implicated in polarity loss-induced metastatic tumor formation in the wing discs (Bunker et al., 2015; Igaki et al., 2006; Külshammer et al., 2015; Uhlirova and Bohmann, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Significant upregulation of grnd, Jra, and Mmp1 was detected in ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells compared to tjTS experimental control ovaries.
source: Compared to the tjTS experimental control ovaries, we detected significant upregulation of grnd (GAPDH-normalized expression relative to the experimental control: 2.84 ± 0.122 standard error; p=0.0002), Jra (1.62 ± 0.059; p=0.0086), and Mmp1 (2.79 ± 0.129; p=0.0002) and noticeable upregulation of Ets21C (1.88 ± 0.35; p=0.0861) and kay (1.58 ± 0.188; p=0.0837) in ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Noticeable upregulation of Ets21C and kay was detected in ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells.
source: Compared to the tjTS experimental control ovaries, we detected significant upregulation of grnd (GAPDH-normalized expression relative to the experimental control: 2.84 ± 0.122 standard error; p=0.0002), Jra (1.62 ± 0.059; p=0.0086), and Mmp1 (2.79 ± 0.129; p=0.0002) and noticeable upregulation of Ets21C (1.88 ± 0.35; p=0.0861) and kay (1.58 ± 0.188; p=0.0837) in ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Both clusters 7 and 8 exhibit Jra, kay, and grnd enrichment.
source: Mapping the expression of Ets21C, grnd, Jra, and kay to specific Lgl-KD follicle cell clusters, we found that while both clusters 7 and 8 exhibit Jra, kay, and grnd enrichment, Ets21C is specifically detected in cluster 7, the terminal states of which also overlapped with dynamic Mmp1 expression (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene enrichment plots shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Ets21C is specifically detected in cluster 7.
source: Mapping the expression of Ets21C, grnd, Jra, and kay to specific Lgl-KD follicle cell clusters, we found that while both clusters 7 and 8 exhibit Jra, kay, and grnd enrichment, Ets21C is specifically detected in cluster 7, the terminal states of which also overlapped with dynamic Mmp1 expression (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene enrichment plots shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The terminal states of cluster 7 overlapped with dynamic Mmp1 expression.
source: Mapping the expression of Ets21C, grnd, Jra, and kay to specific Lgl-KD follicle cell clusters, we found that while both clusters 7 and 8 exhibit Jra, kay, and grnd enrichment, Ets21C is specifically detected in cluster 7, the terminal states of which also overlapped with dynamic Mmp1 expression (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene enrichment plots and RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cluster 7 consists of heterogenous tumorigenic cells.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that cluster 7 consists of heterogenous tumorigenic cells, which could be further divided into transcriptomically homogenous groups to identify markers that could help us detect the precise location of these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple analytical approaches.

claim: Cluster 7 was subdivided into five transcriptomically similar neighborhoods.
source: To explore cluster 7 heterogeneity, we subdivided its 1144 cells even further and obtained five transcriptomically similar neighborhoods (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by subclustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Clusters 7_0 and 7_2 were the 'roots' of the inferred lineage that terminated into cluster 7_1.
source: From the stream of velocity vectors superimposed on the cells embedded on UMAP space, we deduced that clusters 7_0 (293 cells) and 7_2 (193 cells) were the 'roots' of the inferred lineage that terminated into cluster 7_1 (291 cells), while clusters 7_3 (191 cells) and 7_4 (176 cells) were the intermediate states of transcriptional transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA velocity analysis.

claim: Clusters 7_3 and 7_4 were the intermediate states of transcriptional transition.
source: From the stream of velocity vectors superimposed on the cells embedded on UMAP space, we deduced that clusters 7_0 (293 cells) and 7_2 (193 cells) were the 'roots' of the inferred lineage that terminated into cluster 7_1 (291 cells), while clusters 7_3 (191 cells) and 7_4 (176 cells) were the intermediate states of transcriptional transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA velocity analysis.

claim: The regulons could be organized into two larger clusters based on hierarchical clustering.
source: To describe the regulatory relationships of TFs in all cluster 7 cells, we evaluated which of them might cooperate with each other by assessing the Connection Specificity Index (CSI) metric (Fuxman Bass et al., 2013). Hierarchically clustering the 16 regulons active in cluster 7 (including those that are suffixed '_extended' since they incorporate low-confidence TF associations and are inclusive of more genes), we inferred that the regulons could be organized into two larger clusters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by CSI analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: One cluster of highly correlated regulons contained both the AP-1 TF heterodimers Jra and kay along with Usf, ftz-f1 and srp.
source: One of these highly correlated clusters contained both the AP-1 TF heterodimers Jra and kay along with the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) TF Usf, ftz transcription factor 1 (ftz-f1) and the GATA-binding TF serpent (srp).
evidence: This is supported by CSI analysis.

claim: The other cluster included Atf3, Hr4, Hnf4, hairy, CrebA, and Ets21C.
source: The other cluster included the AP-1 interacting gene activating transcription factor 3 (Atf3), nuclear receptor TFs hormone receptor 4 (Hr4), hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 (Hnf4), the bHLH transcriptional repressor hairy (h), cyclic-AMP response element binding protein A (CrebA), and Ets21C.
evidence: This is supported by CSI analysis.

claim: Highly cooperative regulons showed similar extent of enrichment for each cluster.
source: Furthermore, when the relative activity of these regulons was compared between clusters, highly cooperative regulons showed similar extent of enrichment for each cluster (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by regulon activity comparison shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Regulons associated with TFs Jra and kay showed low activity in clusters representing earlier timepoints, intermediate enrichment in transitioning clusters and high activity in the terminal cluster.
source: For example, regulons associated with TFs Jra and kay showed low activity in clusters representing earlier timepoints, intermediate enrichment in the transitioning clusters and high activity in the terminal cluster.
evidence: This is supported by regulon activity comparison.

claim: The Ets21C regulon exhibited a pattern that was opposite to that shown by the AP-1 TFs.
source: Similarly, the Ets21C regulon exhibit a pattern that was opposite to that shown by the AP-1 TFs.
evidence: This is supported by regulon activity comparison.

claim: The comprehensive analytical approach identified processes specific to individual cells and resolved regulon activity over time as experienced by transitioning cluster 7 cells.
source: Overall, our comprehensive analytical approach not only identified processes specific to individual cells but also resolved regulon activity over time, as was experienced by the transitioning cluster 7 cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the analytical approach and its results.

claim: Cluster 7_0 was annotated as mature, postmitotic follicle cells based on Yp1-3+ and Vm26Ab+ marker expression.
source: Detecting specific markers, we annotated cluster 7_0 as mature, postmitotic follicle cells (Yp1-3+ and Vm26Ab+) and cluster 7_2 as immature, mitotic follicle cells (stg+, Myc+, and HmgD+), while cluster 7_1 expressed markers involved in apoptotic cell clearance (drpr+ and crq+) representing the degenerated egg chambers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cluster 7_2 was annotated as immature, mitotic follicle cells based on stg+, Myc+, and HmgD+ marker expression.
source: Detecting specific markers, we annotated cluster 7_0 as mature, postmitotic follicle cells (Yp1-3+ and Vm26Ab+) and cluster 7_2 as immature, mitotic follicle cells (stg+, Myc+, and HmgD+), while cluster 7_1 expressed markers involved in apoptotic cell clearance (drpr+ and crq+) representing the degenerated egg chambers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cluster 7_1 expressed markers involved in apoptotic cell clearance representing the degenerated egg chambers.
source: Detecting specific markers, we annotated cluster 7_0 as mature, postmitotic follicle cells (Yp1-3+ and Vm26Ab+) and cluster 7_2 as immature, mitotic follicle cells (stg+, Myc+, and HmgD+), while cluster 7_1 expressed markers involved in apoptotic cell clearance (drpr+ and crq+) representing the degenerated egg chambers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Clusters 7_0, 7_2, and 7_1 were hypothesized to comprise the heterogenous multilayer.
source: This conclusion was in agreement with the assignment of clusters 7_0 and 7_2 as 'roots' and 7_1 as the 'terminal' state, and we hypothesized that these cells were those that comprised the heterogenous multilayer.
evidence: This is an inference based on lineage analysis and marker expression.

claim: Cluster 7_3 was composed of cells that transitioned from the mature cell cluster 7_0.
source: We were particularly interested in identifying the differentially enriched markers of cluster 7_3, which were composed of cells that transitioned from the mature cell cluster 7_0, as the underlying gene expression in them would likely represent the multilayered cells at the leading edge, given that the invasive front is composed of delaminating postmitotic follicle cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on lineage analysis.

claim: The underlying gene expression in cluster 7_3 would likely represent the multilayered cells at the leading edge.
source: We were particularly interested in identifying the differentially enriched markers of cluster 7_3, which were composed of cells that transitioned from the mature cell cluster 7_0, as the underlying gene expression in them would likely represent the multilayered cells at the leading edge, given that the invasive front is composed of delaminating postmitotic follicle cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on lineage analysis and biological knowledge.

claim: Several relatively enriched markers of cluster 7_3 associated with the actomyosin cytoskeleton, glutathione metabolic process, Rab protein signal transduction, and lysosomal trafficking pathway were found.
source: We found several relatively enriched markers of cluster 7_3 that associated with the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Act5C, Act42A, Vinc, capt, cib and sqh and Mlc-c), and were part of the glutathione metabolic process (GstD1, GstD2, and GstD3), Rab protein signal transduction (Rab1, Rab7, and RabX), as well as the lysosomal trafficking pathway (Rab7, cathD, Cp1, Cln3, and Swim) (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis.

claim: Genes coding for the cytosolic glutathione S-transferase family proteins are expressed under the control of the TF cap-n-collar (Drosophila Nrf2 homolog).
source: Genes coding for the cytosolic glutathione S-transferase (Gst) family proteins are expressed under the control of the TF cap-n-collar or cnc (Drosophila Nrf2 homolog) (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008), which was also present within the regulons of TFs Jra, kay, Usf, as well as Atf3 (Source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cnc was present within the regulons of TFs Jra, kay, Usf, as well as Atf3.
source: Genes coding for the cytosolic glutathione S-transferase (Gst) family proteins are expressed under the control of the TF cap-n-collar or cnc (Drosophila Nrf2 homolog) (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008), which was also present within the regulons of TFs Jra, kay, Usf, as well as Atf3 (Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by regulon analysis.

claim: Cluster 7_3 likely represented cells with elevated activation of the cnc-driven, stress-responsive Keap1-Nrf2 signaling pathway.
source: From our results, we concluded that cluster 7_3 likely represented cells with elevated activation of the cnc-driven, stress-responsive Keap1-Nrf2 signaling pathway (Yamamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on marker expression analysis and citations to previous literature.

claim: Enrichment of cnc and its endogenous inhibitor Keap1 was detected in clusters 7 and 8 of the Lgl-KD dataset.
source: We detected an enrichment of cnc and its endogenous inhibitor Keap1 in clusters 7 and 8 of the Lgl-KD dataset (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by gene enrichment plots shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RNA velocity analysis detected the dynamic behavior of Keap1 as well as several Gst genes.
source: In support of the transient expression inferred from detecting the elevated expression of Keap1-Nrf2 pathway target genes in cluster 7_3, RNA velocity analysis detected the dynamic behavior of Keap1 as well as several Gst genes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Infrequent β-gal activity was detected in subsets of cells within the multilayer using the GstD-lacZ enhancer trap reporter assay.
source: Using the GstD-lacZ enhancer trap reporter assay to validate Keap1-Nrf2 signaling activation (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008), we detected infrequent β-gal activity in subsets of cells within the multilayer (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by β-gal staining shown in Figure 4G and citations to previous literature.

claim: Cluster 7 represented the heterogenous cells of the multilayer, where dynamic activation of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling was detected in a smaller subset of those cells.
source: We were therefore able to conclude that cluster 7 indeed represented the heterogenous cells of the multilayer, where the dynamic activation of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling was detected in a smaller subset of those cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple analytical approaches and validation experiments.

claim: In ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells, 86.35% ovarioles contained egg chambers with more than two layers of cells at mid-oogenesis.
source: In ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells, 86.35% (N = 793) ovarioles contained egg chambers with more than two layers of cells at mid-oogenesis, whereas Lgl-KD+Cnc-KD ovaries exhibited comparable multilayering in only 27.2% ovarioles (N = 964).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis.

claim: Lgl-KD+Cnc-KD ovaries exhibited comparable multilayering in only 27.2% ovarioles.
source: In ovaries with Lgl-KD follicle cells, 86.35% (N = 793) ovarioles contained egg chambers with more than two layers of cells at mid-oogenesis, whereas Lgl-KD+Cnc-KD ovaries exhibited comparable multilayering in only 27.2% ovarioles (N = 964).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis.

claim: Keap1-KD in Lgl-KD follicle cells exhibited a partial rescue of the Lgl-KD phenotype as only 35.46% ovarioles contained egg chambers with comparable multilayering.
source: Keap1-KD in Lgl-KD follicle cells exhibited a partial rescue of the Lgl-KD phenotype as only 35.46% ovarioles (N = 897) contained egg chambers with comparable multilayering.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative phenotypic analysis.

claim: In both Lgl-KD+Cnc-KD and Lgl-KD+Keap1-KD conditions, the timing of germline cell death was delayed resulting in development to proceed and form intact stage 10 egg chambers.
source: In both conditions, the timing of germline cell death was delayed resulting in development to proceed and form intact stage 10 egg chambers.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations.

claim: Stage 10 egg chambers in Lgl-KD+Cnc-KD and Lgl-KD+Keap1-KD conditions continued to exhibit border cell migration defects.
source: These egg chambers continued to exhibit border cell migration defects, indicating that knocking down Cnc or Keap1 did not rescue the cell-autonomous defects of Lgl-KD cells and instead were negatively regulating some aspect of multilayer growth itself (Figure 5A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knocking down Cnc or Keap1 did not rescue the cell-autonomous defects of Lgl-KD cells and instead were negatively regulating some aspect of multilayer growth itself.
source: These egg chambers continued to exhibit border cell migration defects, indicating that knocking down Cnc or Keap1 did not rescue the cell-autonomous defects of Lgl-KD cells and instead were negatively regulating some aspect of multilayer growth itself (Figure 5A, arrowheads).
evidence: This is an inference based on phenotypic observations.

claim: The reduction in Lgl-KD multilayering was not caused by increased cytotoxicity induced by elevated oxidative stress following Keap1-Nrf2 signaling disruption as apoptosis was rarely observed in these cells.
source: This reduction in Lgl-KD multilayering was also not caused by increased cytotoxicity induced by elevated oxidative stress following Keap1-Nrf2 signaling disruption as apoptosis was rarely observed in these cells (Dcp-1 staining not shown), thereby necessitating an alternate explanation for the rescue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of apoptosis markers.

claim: In the absence of Lgl-KD, either overexpression or knockdown of Keap1 did not significantly affect the levels of cnc but caused a decrease in the levels of GstD2.
source: We found that in the absence of Lgl-KD either overexpression or knockdown of Keap1 did not significantly affect the levels of cnc but caused a decrease in the levels of GstD2, the bona fide target of Keap1-Nrf2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: In the presence of Lgl-KD, overexpressing Keap1 caused an increase in GstD2 levels that was comparable to that observed in Lgl-KD alone.
source: In the presence of Lgl-KD, however, overexpressing Keap1 caused an increase in GstD2 levels that was comparable to that observed in Lgl-KD alone.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: In egg chambers with Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE follicle cells, a remarkable worsening of the Lgl-KD phenotype was noticed as the egg chambers appeared both multilayered and increasingly fused.
source: In these egg chambers with Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE follicle cells, we noticed a remarkable worsening of the Lgl-KD phenotype as the egg chambers appeared both multilayered as well as increasingly fused (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Epithelial 'bridging' was observed in several egg chambers (n = 119/185) at midoogenesis with Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE follicle cells.
source: We also observed epithelial 'bridging' in several egg chambers (n = 119/185) at midoogenesis, where the multilayered cells formed invasive inroads through the recesses between germline cells that connected to the lateral epithelia, forming a bridge between two separate sections of the follicular epithelia (Figure 5D, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ectopic expression of UAS-CncC resulted in some enhancement of the Lgl-KD multilayering as well as fused egg chambers at early oogenesis (N = 39/121).
source: While ectopic expression of UAS-CncC (longest isoform of wildtype Cnc; Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008) also resulted in some enhancement of the Lgl-KD multilayering as well as fused egg chambers at early oogenesis (N = 39/121), it did not exhibit the 'bridging' phenotype in egg chambers at midoogenesis (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5D and citations to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of UAS-CncC did not exhibit the 'bridging' phenotype in egg chambers at midoogenesis.
source: While ectopic expression of UAS-CncC (longest isoform of wildtype Cnc; Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008) also resulted in some enhancement of the Lgl-KD multilayering as well as fused egg chambers at early oogenesis (N = 39/121), it did not exhibit the 'bridging' phenotype in egg chambers at midoogenesis (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The fused egg chamber phenotype occurred due to increased invasiveness, not as a consequence of two individualized egg chambers fusing at the ends due to improper stalk cell differentiation.
source: However, that the fused egg chamber phenotype occurred due to increased invasiveness, and not as a consequence of two individualized egg chambers fusing at the ends due to improper stalk cell differentiation, was evident from the observation that nurse cell nuclei were abnormally compressed by the invasive fronts of collectively migrating Lgl-KD+CncC-OE follicle cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on confocal imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Phenotypic enhancement in Lgl-KD+CncC-OE was verified by observing increased multilayer formation in egg chambers at midoogenesis in 22.85% intact ovarioles at 2 days after heat shock induction.
source: Phenotypic enhancement in Lgl-KD+CncC-OE was also verified by observing increased multilayer formation in egg chambers at midoogenesis in 22.85% intact ovarioles (N = 16/70) at 2 days after heat shock (AHS) induction, which is an insufficient amount of time for Lgl-KD to exhibit multilayering (only 2% egg chambers showed multilayering; N = 50 ovarioles) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CncC-mediated enhancement is partially caused by the autonomous activation of Keap1 in the UAS-CncC-expressing cells.
source: We believe that the CncC-mediated enhancement is partially caused by the autonomous activation of Keap1 in the UAS-CncC-expressing cells (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008) and that the increased egg chamber fusion is a phenotype specific to the earlier developmental stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and citations to previous literature.

claim: The increased egg chamber fusion is a phenotype specific to the earlier developmental stages.
source: We believe that the CncC-mediated enhancement is partially caused by the autonomous activation of Keap1 in the UAS-CncC-expressing cells (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008) and that the increased egg chamber fusion is a phenotype specific to the earlier developmental stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: The increased invasiveness of Lgl-KD by Keap1 overexpression was likely controlled by the noncanonical functions of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling outside its role in oxidative stress response.
source: Nonetheless, given that the invasive phenotype was not regulated by antagonizing functions of Keap1 and Cnc, the increased invasiveness of Lgl-KD by Keap1 overexpression was likely controlled by the noncanonical functions of Keap1-Nrf2 signaling outside its role in oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: Gaps were noticed within the multilayers in egg chambers with Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE or Lgl-KD+CncC-OE enhanced invasion, indicating a probable loss of cell–cell adhesion.
source: Unlike the Lgl-KD multilayers, in the egg chambers with Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE or Lgl-KD+CncC-OE enhanced invasion, we noticed gaps within the multilayers, indicating a probable loss of cell–cell adhesion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on confocal imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE egg chambers, a relative decrease in Shg and Arm enrichment was detected at the junctions of apically invading multilayered cells when compared to that in the basal-most layer.
source: In Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE egg chambers, a relative decrease in Shg and Arm enrichment was detected at the junctions of apically invading multilayered cells when compared to that in the basal-most layer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The delaminated Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE cells did not exhibit a complete loss of cell–cell adhesion as Shg and Arm staining continued to be present at cell–cell junctions.
source: However, the delaminated Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE cells did not exhibit a complete loss of cell–cell adhesion as Shg and Arm staining continued to be present at cell–cell junctions.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging.

claim: The delaminated Lgl-KD+Keap1-OE cells maintained cellular junctions, explaining their collective mode of invasion.
source: This observation implied that these cells maintained cellular junctions, thereby explaining their collective mode of invasion and requiring alternate explanations for the occurrence of gaps.
evidence: This is an inference based on imaging observations.

claim: Elevating Keap1 in Lgl-KD background induced a significant (p=0.02) but variable increase (40.3%; N = 10 egg chambers at stage 8) in the delaminated epithelial volume compared to that of the Lgl-KD (21.8%; N = 9) alone.
source: We found that elevating Keap1 in Lgl-KD background induced a significant (p=0.02) but variable increase (40.3%; N = 10 egg chambers at stage 8) in the delaminated epithelial volume compared to that of the Lgl-KD (21.8%; N = 9) alone (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative volume measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 was not detected within the invading cells of the multilayered epithelia.
source: Indeed, mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 (pH3) was also not detected within the invading cells of the multilayered epithelia (Figure 6C, middle panel), further suggesting that the increase in invasive epithelial volume was not caused primarily by overproliferating cells pushing out the delaminating epithelia.
evidence: This is supported by pH3 staining shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The increase in invasive epithelial volume was not caused primarily by overproliferating cells pushing out the delaminating epithelia.
source: Indeed, mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 (pH3) was also not detected within the invading cells of the multilayered epithelia (Figure 6C, middle panel), further suggesting that the increase in invasive epithelial volume was not caused primarily by overproliferating cells pushing out the delaminating epithelia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of pH3 staining.

claim: The phenotype was likely caused by an enhancement of invasive behavior.
source: Instead, this phenotype was likely caused by an enhancement of invasive behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations.

claim: Dynamic behavior of several genes coding for proteins that mediate interactions between integrins and filamentous actin was detected in cluster 7 cells.
